en.title: Days and months
en.goal: Say the days of the week and the months, and arrange to meet someone.

lessons.dias-da-semana: Days of the week and today

phrases.scenario: You've lost track of the day of the week. What do you ask?
Someone asks what day it is, and it's Monday. What do you answer?
Someone asks which month your birthday is in — March. What do you say?
You're saying goodbye to a coworker and you'll see them again tomorrow. What do you say?

phrases.t: Next week, I'm going on a trip.
The month of January is very cold.

dialogue.title: Arranging to meet
lines: Tuesday, does that work for you?
No, I work on Tuesday. What about Wednesday?

a-demain-vs-a-bientot.title: "À demain" or "à bientôt"?
a-demain-vs-a-bientot.body: French goodbyes vary depending on how long until you meet again: à demain when you know you'll see the person tomorrow, and à bientôt when the reunion is more uncertain, just "see you soon". Au revoir, on the other hand, is neutral and works for any goodbye, without saying when the next meeting will be.

dias-semana-deuses-romanos.title: Where do the names of the days of the week come from?
dias-semana-deuses-romanos.body: The French days of the week come from Roman gods/planets: lundi is the day of the Moon (Lune), mardi is the day of Mars (Mars). The pattern continues: mercredi (Mercury), jeudi (Jupiter), vendredi (Venus), samedi (Saturn) — only dimanche breaks the rule, coming from the Latin for "the Lord's day".

nous-sommes-on-est.title: "Nous sommes lundi" becomes "On est lundi" in everyday speech
nous-sommes-on-est.body: In everyday speech, on has practically replaced nous as "we" — on est lundi instead of "nous sommes lundi". The verb conjugates like "il/elle" (on est, on a, on va), not like "nous". In the exercises here, keep using "nous" — it's the form the exercises ask for.

review.why: FR 'Quel jour sommes-nous ?' is formal-ish; EN also 'What day is today?'
FR 'il fait beau' = the weather is nice; PT 'está bonito' is vague, so I made the weather explicit
'on est lundi' also fits 'we're on Monday'; chose the natural 'it's Monday'
PT 'a gente' has no EN equivalent; collapsed to 'we'
Latin 'dies Dominicus'; 'the Lord's day' is the standard rendering
